metadata.title: Use of a domain-specific ontology to support automated document categorization at the concept level: Method development and evaluation
metadata.abstract_summary: This study proposes a text categorization method that incorporates a domain-specific ontology to support automated document categorization more effectively. The proposed method classifies documents according to their respective range of relevant concepts and is shown to be more effective than several prevalent benchmarks.

sections.heading: A B S T R A C T
sections.text: Voluminous, conveniently accessible textual documents, created and disseminated by modern information technology, makes automated document organization increasingly important for both individuals and organi­ zations. Many existing techniques rely on document content analysis that classifies new, unlabeled documents by examining the similarity based on the overlap between their important features and the representative features of each document category. However, the performance of feature-based techniques can be significantly hindered by word mismatch and ambiguity problems. As a remedy, this study takes a concept-based approach and propose a text categorization method that incorporates a domain-specific ontology to support automated document cate­ gorization more effectively. The proposed method classifies documents according to their respective range of relevant concepts. We empirically evaluate our method versus several prevalent benchmarks that include feature-based k-nearest neighbors ( k NN) and semantic-based techniques. The results show the proposed method more effective than the benchmark techniques; it achieves better performances when using a complete concept hierarchy without considering the hierarchical relationships among concepts. The proposed method illustrates how to incorporate a domain-specific ontology to improve document classification. Our method is computa­ tionally efficient because it produces a concept space of relatively few dimensionalities and does not require semantic space reconstruction as new documents arrive. Moreover, the relationships and patterns for classifying documents, generated by our method, are explicit and comprehensible. 1. Introduction The ubiquity of information technology (IT) enables easy creation of and convenient access to enormous information, anytime and anywhere. Most information appears in the textual format, such as articles and news wires, which makes effective document organization increasingly important ( Deng, Li, Weng, & Zhang, 2018; Spies & Jungemann-Dorner, 2013 ). Particularly, the availability of online textual doc­ uments — enormous in quantity, complex in structure, and diverse in sources — constitutes a critical challenge to both individuals and orga­ nizations when they organize these documents into distinct categories. While manual document classification has become ineffective and impractical, the automated categorization approach has to acknowledge that document classification is intrinsically subjective, marked by observable differences in how users classify the same set of documents ( Deng et al., 2018; Sebastiani, 2002 ). 1 This subjective nature in turn indicates the need to categorize documents in congruence with the classification preferences of the focal user or organization. Effective document classification is also central to organizational information management, knowledge management, business intelli­ gence, and environmental surveillance ( Boella et al., 2016; Chung, 2014 ), especially as online documents are created at an accelerating pace ( Spies & Jungemann-Dorner, 2013 ). Automated text categorization can support document management ( Aggarwal & Zhai, 2012; Sebas­ tiani, 2002; Wei, Yang, Lee, Shi, & Yang, 2014 ). As Shang et al. sections.heading: Expert Systems With Applications
sections.text: journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/eswa https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eswa.2021.114681 Received 29 April 2020; Received in revised form 28 September 2020; Accepted 3 February 2021 Expert Systems With Applications 174 (2021) 114681 2 management in organizations, and it requires effective algorithms and computational methods to improve classification accuracy and effi­ ciency. Overall, text categorization involves the use of supervised or semi-supervised learning to identify or infer from previously labeled documents patterns or rules that can be used to classify new, unlabeled documents into adequate categories ( Aggarwal & Zhai, 2012; Khan, Baharudin, Lee, & Khan, 2010; Lee, Hu, Cheng, & Hsieh, 2012 ). Previous research has taken different approaches toward document categorization. Many existing techniques rely on document content analysis ( Aggarwal & Zhai, 2012; Qu et al., 2018; Rehman, Javed, & Babri, 2017; Sebastiani, 2002 ). Typically, this approach infers a classi­ fication model from previously classified documents and then uses the resulting model (classifier) to determine the most adequate category to which a new, unlabeled document belongs, according to the similarity between the representative features of the respective document cate­ gories and those of the new document. However, similarity measures built on the representative features of different document categories could become ineffective for classifying new documents, especially in the presence of word mismatch (synonymy) and ambiguity (polysemy) problems ( Kim, Kim, & Cho, 2017 ). For example, existing feature-based techniques may regard “ classification ” and “ categorization ” as different terms, despite their highly similar or even identical semantic connota­ tion. Also, these techniques could fail to distinguish “ apple ” as it refers to a fruit versus an IT company. Previous research has addressed such word mismatch problems by employing latent semantic analysis (LSA) ( Deerwester, Dumais, Furnas, Landauer, & Harshman, 1990 ), a statistical method that analyzes the underlying term correlation structure in a document corpus ( Xu & Croft, 2000 ). In general, LSA applies singular value decomposition (SVD) to construct a new semantic space for a set of documents, then maps them within the resulting space ( Furnas et al., 1988 ). Although LSA seems effective for coping with word mismatch problems, its use requires substantial computational processing to reconstruct the semantic space embedded in the accumulating classified documents. The processing requirement can significantly escalate with the quantity of documents. In addition, the constructed semantic space only represents term – document relationships in the original document corpus; it pro­ vides a less effective basis for document classification, because the newly created space cannot reveal the underlying relationship between a document and the category to which it belongs. Several studies use word embeddings, such as doc2vec, to analyze the contextual informa­ tion of words and documents, and thus capture their semantic or syn­ tactic properties to represent documents as vectors. Documents with similar contextual information are located close to one another in the embedded space. Although a word embedding model appears effective for text categorization ( Dai, Olah, & Le, 2015 ), it is difficult to interpret the classification results, because the document vectors resulting from word embeddings are generated by neural networks and thus not easily interpretable ( Kim et al., 2017; Li, Mao, Xu, Li, & Zhang, 2020 ). To address the inherent limitations of feature-based text categori­ zation while coping with word mismatch and ambiguity problems, we take a concept-based approach to extend the feature-based approach by incorporating a domain-specific ontology. Although many less relevant features are filtered and removed in the feature selection phase, the number of representative Y.-H. Lee et al. Expert Systems With Applications 174 (2021) 114681 3 features still can be overwhelming, which demands substantial compu­ tational processing and affects classification accuracy and efficiency negatively ( Bilski, 2011; Khan et al., 2010; Uysal & Gunal, 2014b ). Moreover, because feature-based techniques often compare the essential features of unlabeled documents against those of the predefined docu­ ment categories at a lexical level, they have difficulty coping with word mismatch and ambiguity problems. 2.2. Document representations for text categorization To mitigate feature-based techniques ’ limitations associated with the high dimensionality of the representative feature space as well as addressing word mismatch and ambiguity problems, previous studies have applied bag-of-concepts (BoC) document representation for text categorization, with which each document is represented by a weighted bag of concepts. For example, Sahlgren and C ¨ oster (2004) develop a BoC-based technique to produce context vectors for words on the basis of their cooccurrences and then use these vectors to represent docu­ ments for text categorization. Kim et al. (2017) propose a BoC document representation that evolves concepts by clustering word vectors pro­ duced from word2vec and representing documents as concept vectors using the evolved concepts clusters, together with their respective fre­ quencies. Li et al. (2020) develop a BoC model for document represen­ tation and a concept score-inverse soft document frequency weighting scheme to identify documents of higher-level semantics. A BoC model can use the conceptual knowledge, automatically ob­ tained form an external knowledge base, to capture the semantic relat­ edness and conceptual information of textual documents for improved document classification. Toward that end, LSA represents a popular model to discover latent semantic structures of documents and trans­ form them into a substantially reduced dimension space and dense se­ mantic (concept) vectors ( Deerwester et al., 1990 ). In general, LSA analyzes term correlation structures to identify common usage patterns of different words in a document corpus for improved document clas­ sification performance ( Deerwester et al., 1990; Meng, Lin, & Yu, 2011 ). Typically, LSA applies singular value decomposition (SVD) to create a term-document matrix that can construct a new semantic space, or the LSA space. Closely associated terms and documents then get re- represented in the same semantic space ( Deerwester et al., 1990; Kon­ tostathis & Pottenger, 2006 ). Thus, LSA reduces the dimensionality of feature vectors for text categorization ( Zhang, Yoshida, & Tang, 2011 ). In addition, word embeddings have attracted increasing attention recently. Word embedding, a distributed representation for words, uti­ lizes contextual information of each word and captures the semantic and syntactic properties of different words in a low-dimensional, dense space ( Bengio, Ducharme, Vincent, & Janvin, 2003 ). Concept mapping functions to measure the similarity between a document d i and each concept o j in the domain- specific ontology, and to convert documents from feature-based to concept-based representations. With the domain-specific ontology, we can measure the degree of relevance between a document and each concept in that ontology. We define a weighting function for the degree of relevance between a document d i and a concept o j as w m ( d i , o j ) = ∑ f k ∈ o j ( w c ( f k , o j ) × TF ( d i , o j ) ) × pf ij , where f k is the concept descriptor derived by the OE approach that belongs to o j , w c ( f k , o j ) indicates the weight of f k in o j , TF ( f k , d i ) refers to the within-document term frequency of f k in d i , and pf ij denotes the percentage of concept descriptors that belong to o j and appear in d i . We assume that the more concept descriptors that appear in a document, the more closely that document relates to that concept. We further consider the percentage of concept descriptors of o j appearing in a document to avoid dominance by a few frequent concept descriptors. After concept mapping, each document is represented as a set of con­ cepts, together with their respective degrees of relevance. 3.2. Document Re-representation In the document re-representation phase, the OCTC method selects representative concepts from the training documents with known cate­ gories and then uses these selected concepts to represent each document, training or testing (unlabeled). Both concept selection and document representation occur during this phase. After using concept-based rep­ resentation to transform the documents, in accordance with the domain- specific ontology, concept selection is performed to identify from training documents a set of representative concepts. To measure the discriminatory power of a concept in relation to the training documents, the OCTC method uses a weighting average χ 2 statistic measure, calcu­ lated as χ 2 avg ( o j ) = ∑ C i ∈ M ( p ( C i ) × χ 2 ( C i , o j )) , where p ( C i ) is the number of documents in C i divided by the total number of training documents. The top k concepts with the highest average χ 2 statistic scores then serve as representative concepts. Next, the OCTC method performs document representation, using the selected representative concepts to represent each document, training or testing (unlabeled), as a concept vector with specific weights. Three weighting schemes are considered: binary (presence versus absence of a concept in a document), within- document concept frequency (frequency of the descriptors of a concept appearing in a document), and weighting (document-concept similarity, measured by the weighting function of the relevance between a document and a concept). Finally, we take a parameter-tuning approach ( Yang, 1999 ) to determine the representation scheme. 3.3. Document categorization With training and unlabeled documents represented by the selected representative concepts, the proposed method classifies each unlabeled document into an appropriate category, using the k NN technique, which appears effective and robust for multi-class classification tasks ( Hota & Pathak, 2018; Yang, 1999 ), is easy to implement and can be applied in various document categorization scenarios ( Bilski, 2011; Khan et al., 2010; Pang & Jiang, 2013; Sebastiani, 2002 ). For each unlabeled document, the OCTC method uses cosine similarity to assess the simi­ larity between the unlabeled document and all the training documents; the k training documents most similar to the unlabeled document then get selected. claims.text: The proposed Ontology-Enabled Concept-Based Text Categorization (OCTC) method uses a domain-specific ontology to support automated document categorization.
The OCTC method classifies documents according to their respective range of relevant concepts, which are extracted using a phrase parser and concept mapping functions.
The degree of relevance between a document and each concept in the ontology is measured using a weighting function.
The OCTC method is more effective than benchmark techniques, including feature-based k-nearest neighbors and semantic-based techniques.

sections.text: We performed a series of parameter tuning analyses. We followed Lee, Wei, and Hu (2011) to construct the ontology, set the number of concept descriptors at level one ( k cd ) to 20 and the increment of concept descriptors at the next level ( δ cd ) to 10. Next, we analyzed the com­ monality threshold ( α p ) over a range of 6% – 14% (in increments of 2%), with α p = 100% indicating no concept refinement, and set α p to 6% in the evaluation. We examined the representation schemes for both the OCTC method and feature-based k NN baseline, and decided to adopt term frequency as the document representation scheme for feature-based k NN and concept weighting for OCTC, according to the analysis results. Several parameters are important: the number of concepts ( k c ) for OCTC, the number of representative features ( k f ) for feature-based k NN, the number of spaces ( k s ) for LSA-based k NN, and the number of dimensions ( k d ) for doc2vec-based k NN. We randomly selected the classification results by 10 different users to fine-tune these parameters and set k c at 300, k f at 4000, k s at 200, and k d at 260, according to the analysis results. Moreover, two models, distributed memory (DM) and distributed bag of words (DBoW), are proposed for doc2vec to learn paragraphs and document embeddings ( Le & Mikolov, 2014 ). In this study, we used the DM model because of its effectiveness for learning document embed­ dings in text categorization ( Le & Mikolov, 2014; Li et al., 2020 ). 5. Evaluation results and further analyses With the parameter values selected from the parameter-tuning analysis results, we examined the performance of the OCTC method versus the benchmarks (feature-based k NN, LSA-based k NN, and doc2vec-based k NN). We evaluated each over the range from 1 to 65 neighbors, in increments of 5, by examining its classification accuracy. As we present in Fig. 3 , both OCTC and LSA-based k NN noticeably outperformed feature-based k NN and doc2vec-based k NN. The proposed method ’ s accuracy exceeds 60% and is consistently higher than that of LSA-based k NN, across the different numbers of neighbors under ex­ amination. Although the accuracy of doc2vec-based k NN decreases as the number of neighbors increases, it still outperforms the feature-based k NN substantially. We performed a vis- ` a-vis analysis to compare the best performance achieved by the respective techniques, and used the results to examine the statistical significance of their performance differentials. As shown in Fig. 3 , OCTC (0.662), LSA-based k NN (0.644), doc2vec- based k NN (0.573), and feature-based k NN (0.526) recorded the best performance when the number of neighbors equaled 25, 15, 1, and 10, respectively. Two-tailed t -test results show that the classification accu­ racy of the proposed OCTC method is significantly higher than that of LSA-, doc2vec-, or feature-based k NN, with p < .01. Jointly, these evaluation results indicate that our method outperforms all the bench­ mark techniques. We further compared the performances of OCTC versus different combinations of document representation schemes (such as LSA and doc2vec) and learning algorithms that include support vector machine (SVM) and logistic regression (LR). As we summarize in Table 2 , the OCTC method ’ s prediction accuracy is comparable to that of LSA-based SVM and is higher than that of any benchmark technique.
